directions.title: Replace the torch path with a fused FlyDSL a4w4 MoE: route/sort, x→MXFP4 quant, stage 1 (gate+up, clamped SwiGLU, MXFP4 requant), stage 2 (down × routing weight), using native scaled fp4 MFMA on the 16x16-preshuffled weights
directions.hypothesis: The 12.5 ms all-expert bf16 dequant, the ~20-pass torch _mxfp4 and the glue (slab gathers, fp32 combine matmul) make up 95%+ of the 16–63 ms. A 3–4 launch FlyDSL pipeline that reads the shuffled fp4 weights straight into mfma_scale_f32_16x16x128_f8f6f4 operands should reach about the baseline's 0.18–2.5 ms. It must reproduce the reference rounding exactly: x rounded to MXFP4 per 1×32, E8M0 = floor(log2 amax) − 2 (+1 if mantissa > 0.75), round-to-nearest-even on e2m1, and y rounded to bf16 then MXFP4. Port aiter's mxfp4_gemm1/mxfp4_gemm2/moe_sorting as the starting point.
directions.priority_reason: Report §5: 26–90× headroom against the candidate. A structurally correct fused kernel takes the score from ~0.016 to ~0.8–1.1. Native fp4 MFMA is needed to match or beat aiter at 3112–32768, where the bf16-dequant practical floor is at or above the baseline.

directions.title: Stepping stone: replace _unpack's 6-pass dequant chain and the ~20-pass torch _mxfp4 with one vectorized FlyDSL kernel each, keeping the rest of the torch path
directions.hypothesis: One FlyDSL dequant kernel at ≥4 TB/s instead of six torch passes at 1–2 TB/s saves about 11 ms per call. A single-pass fused MXFP4 quant kernel with exact reference rounding saves 1–24 ms. Together they cut 16→~5 ms at n=256 and 63→~25 ms at 32768. The quant kernel is reusable as stage (b) of direction 1, and its bit-exact rounding test de-risks direction 1.
directions.priority_reason: Report §6.5: each piece is a 3–5× gain at most. It does not reach 0.1 speedup but is a quick, low-risk landing if the fused kernel slips.

directions.title: Per-regime tile-M equal to the sort unit: BM=32 at n≤640, BM=128 at 3112/3816, BM=128–256 at ≥10000
directions.hypothesis: Weight traffic is M-tiles × weight slab. At n≤640, BM=32 gives exactly one 0.96 GB sweep (≤31 routes per expert), while BM=16 sweeps up to 1.68 GB. At 3816, BM=128 sweeps 1.15 GB against 2.11 GB at BM=64, and at 32768 8.2 GB against 15.9 GB. aiter runs untuned heuristic BM (t32/t128/t64) everywhere, notably BM=64 at 32768.
directions.priority_reason: Neutral on S (aiter is already at BM=32). Large on the 5 M/L Points, where halving weight sweeps against a 2–6.6×-off-roof baseline could give 1.2–2× on each. That is ~5–8% of the mean score.

directions.title: S-regime grid shape: race tile-N downward (256→128→64) in both stages so 128 experts × (N/BN) blocks fill ≥256 CUs with enough bytes in flight
directions.hypothesis: At n≤640 every expert has about one 32-row block, so the N blocks are the parallelism. Narrower tile-N gave +0.8–1.0% per halving on an a4w4 atomic stage 2. Count workgroups against the 256-CU dispatch round to avoid a mostly empty last round.
directions.priority_reason: The S regime has at most 1.16–1.24× to the hard roof. Grid fill is one of the few levers left on 20 of 25 Points.

directions.title: Weight-load cache policy per regime and per M-block: non-temporal at n≤640, cached when a sorted neighbour block has the same expert, scale loads always cached
directions.hypothesis: At S nothing reuses weights, so non-temporal streaming frees L2 and MALL for activations. At M/L (3–9 blocks per expert), non-temporal W1/W2 cost 26% and 6–9% in the field, so cached loads with same-expert neighbours on one XCD are better. Per-block selection gained 1.8% on an a4w4 decode score.
directions.priority_reason: Field numbers: +1.8% per-block selection, a 6–26% loss if set wrong at multi-block. This is a correctness-free knob with a clear regime flip.

directions.title: XCD-aware tile order plus GROUP_M: keep an expert's row tiles and an M-block's N tiles on one XCD, several row tiles of one expert per column sweep
directions.hypothesis: At 10000–32768 each expert has 272–1110 routes (3–9 BM=128 tiles), so expert slabs are re-read through L2. Dealing M-blocks round-robin over XCDs with their N tiles together, and grouping 2–9 row tiles per expert as the 33-expert kernel does at m≥512, turns repeats into L2 hits. Exit on the raw id before the remap.
directions.priority_reason: Field result: 511→475 µs (−7%) on a fused-MoE stage 1 from the XCD placement. Applies mainly to 5 M/L Points.

directions.title: Compute-leaning main loop for large n: gathered A rows through an XOR-swizzled multi-stage LDS ring prefetched two K-steps ahead, B straight to VGPR, 32x32x64 vs 16x16x128 scaled MFMA, s_setprio around the MFMA block
directions.hypothesis: At 32768 aiter is at 1.5 PF/s against ~4 PF practical MXFP4. A loop that hides the gathered-A latency and the B stream behind back-to-back scaled MFMAs (32x32 atom halves the A/B register traffic per FLOP) should lift stage throughput toward 2–3 PF/s. The delivered K3 MoE ran stage 1 at 1.38× aiter's TF/s.
directions.priority_reason: L Points have 2.6–3.4× paper headroom (report §5). Even 1.3× on 3–5 Points is ~4–6% of the mean.

directions.title: Stage-2 combine: race bf16x2 coalesced atomics into out against fixed-order per-route bf16/fp32 rows plus a separate reduce launch, per regime
directions.hypothesis: With topk=4 every route is local. With 16 local routes the atomic stage 2 was 31–42% slower than split+reduce, but with about 2 routes it was faster. topk=4 sits between, and the answer likely flips between S (a launch matters at ~180 µs) and L (contention on 32768×6144 outputs). Rows must stay bf16/fp32 because of the per-element BaselineRelativeBound, so no fp8 or MXFP4 rows.
directions.priority_reason: Field numbers show a 10–40% swing in stage-2 cost depending on routes per token. Stage 2 is about a third of the call.

directions.title: Stage-1 fused epilogue: clamp/SwiGLU in fp32, bf16 round, MXFP4 quantize with shuffled E8M0 in sorted-row order, staged through LDS for 16-byte stores
directions.hypothesis: Writing y as fp4 plus scales (≈R·408 B), produced in registers and stored with wide coalesced stores, keeps the intermediate off the critical path. Writing it in the exact layout stage 2's A DMA consumes removes any relayout. Poorly vectorized stores of y cost noticeably at large R.
directions.priority_reason: The y traffic is small next to the weights, but at L (R=131k routes) store efficiency and the per-lane quant cost become visible.

directions.title: Cut graph nodes: fold x quantization and the output zeroing into the sort launch (or the sort into stage 1), preload kernargs, read the expert id before the A loads
directions.hypothesis: Each graph node costs ~4 µs under AKLR's timer, about 2% of a ~180 µs S-regime call. aiter runs sort + quant + stage1 + stage2. Folding per-token quant and zeroing into the sort launch removed 6.9–8.0 µs in the field, and merging sort phases gained 1.1%. The route kernel must scale past R=1024 (multi-CTA or looping), unlike the prior art.
directions.priority_reason: On 20 S Points with ≤1.16–1.24× headroom, saving 1–2 nodes (4–8 µs of 180–190 µs) is 2–4%, which may decide serving at 1.03.

directions.title: Persistent or capped grids at large n: launch min(work, k·NUM_CU) workgroups that stride over the device-side tile bound instead of the padded upper-bound grid
directions.hypothesis: The padded upper bound (routes + experts·(BM−1))/BM × N blocks over-launches many empty workgroups at 10000–32768. A persistent loop with a per-tile barrier (or C staged per wave) avoids dispatch waste and tail rounds, and beat one tile per workgroup by 3–5% on a dense GEMM.
directions.priority_reason: A field gain of 3–5% on the stage it applies to, restricted to the 3–5 large Points.

directions.title: Offline-raced per-shape configuration table (BM, BN, waves, cache policy, atomic vs reduce, MFMA atom) chosen from n_tokens inside the functools.cache compile function
directions.hypothesis: aiter runs untuned heuristic configs at every Point. The best tile, cache and reduce choice flips between S, M and L, and across the 256–640 band as the >16-route expert count grows 0→96. A table raced offline per Point, with no timing in run, captures the per-Point optimum without a shape-divergence loss.
directions.priority_reason: Tune last. Per-Point picks typically add 2–5% over one config per regime, and it guards against wins on some Points losing on others (a lost workload rejects the candidate).

directions.title: Skip padding work: send padding rows' A loads out of range (buffer bound returns zero) and skip MFMAs on all-padding sub-tiles
directions.hypothesis: With BM=32 at n≤640, experts have 2–31 routes, so a large fraction of tile rows are padding. Out-of-range A loads for padding rows gained ~1% and 1.7 µs on a stage 2. Skipping MFMAs on padding rows gained 1.6% on a stage 1.
directions.priority_reason: Small field gains of 1–3% per stage, but cheap and helpful on the near-roof S Points.

directions.title: parallel routing sort for n > 1024 (first), then per-regime-tile-m-equal-to-the-sort-unit (a time-boxed race)

Small-n stage 2 as a streaming persistent kernel: resident-slot grid (6 WG/CU × 256) looping over the 6144 tiles, with the next tile's W2 loads issued before the current tile's epilogue/atomics, so the W2 stream never drains between tiles
directions.hypothesis: At n≤640, stage 2 runs 6144 short-lived workgroups in exactly 4 rounds (48 KB of W2 each, persist_m=1). It reads W2 at 6.0–6.4 TB/s while stage 1 reaches 6.5–6.6. Each workgroup's ramp-up and epilogue leaves the HBM queue empty, and the round boundaries add tail time. A persistent loop with cross-tile B prefetch (no barrier, C staged per wave, the form that beat one-tile-per-WG by 3–5% on a dense GEMM) should bring W2 up to stage 1's rate: −3 to −5 µs on ~55 µs. This is the opposite axis to the ledger's tile-N-downward race, and both should be raced against the current setting.
directions.priority_reason: Report §6.2 estimates −3 to −5 µs of a ~170–180 µs call (+2–3%) on all 20 S Points. Discounted because the stage is already near the stream rate.

directions.title: Parallel routing sort at n≤640: replace the one-workgroup serial sort (7.6–9.1 µs on one CU) with a wave-per-expert / bitmask-popcount sort spread over many workgroups
directions.hypothesis: The S-regime sort is a single workgroup looping over R/1024 routes and writing 31 padding rows per expert serially while 255 CUs idle. It sits on the critical path in front of x-quant and stage 1. Field data: a wave per expert instead of a workgroup took a sort from 7.3–7.8 to 6.5 µs, and per-expert bitmasks (LDS atomic OR + popcount + one packed prefix scan) took another from 7.65 to 5.32 µs against a ~4.4 µs node floor. Doing the same here should cut 2–4 µs per call. The kept multi-WG sort for n>1024 is a starting point, but it must not add a launch at small n.
directions.priority_reason: 2–4 µs of 168–182 µs is 1–2% on 20 of 25 Points. Capped by the ~4 µs per-node floor.

directions.title: Stage-2 register plan for M/L: issue A ds_reads one 16-row group ahead to cut VGPRs below 124, then raise resident workgroups from 2 to 3–4 per CU to hide atomic and B latency
directions.hypothesis: Stage 2 at large n uses 124 VGPRs and runs 2 WG/CU (cu_num_mul 2) where LDS (16.6 KB) would allow 4. It reaches only 0.96 PF/s, and ~25–30% of its time is waiting on atomics that miss L2. The KB-matched mechanism (A read per 16-row slice one phase ahead) took a fused-MoE MXFP4 stage 2 from 146 to 122 VGPRs at −3%, and gave −8% on another. Raising cu_num_mul alone did nothing (1278.5 vs 1285.9 µs), so registers are the binding limit. With registers freed, more waves can cover the atomic and B-load latency.
directions.priority_reason: Report §6.3 estimates −8 to −15% of stage 2, which is 40–55% of the call at 10000–32768 and ~45% at 3112/3816. That is ~4–7% on 5 Points.

directions.title: Stage-1 occupancy at M/L: bring the t128 build from 324 VGPRs / 99 KB LDS (1 WG per CU) to 2 WG per CU, and choose tiles so 3112/3816 fill whole dispatch rounds
directions.hypothesis: Stage 1 at n>1024 runs one wave per SIMD at 2.0–2.9 PF/s (31% of nominal). At 3816 its 918 WGs take 3.59 rounds with the last 59% full, which is why stage 1 there loses 10.5 µs to aiter. Reading A per 16-row slice one phase ahead (KB-matched: 202→148 VGPRs, +7.5% on a t64 MXFP4 stage 1) plus a shallower or narrower LDS stage would let 2 WGs share a CU and overlap one's epilogue with the other's MFMAs. A tile choice that makes WGs a multiple of resident slots removes the partial round at 3816.
directions.priority_reason: Report §6.4 estimates −5 to −10% of stage 1, which is ~45% of the call, on 5 Points: ~2–4.5% each.

directions.title: Stage-2 tile order for output-atomic locality at L: sweep column slabs outermost (all experts' M-blocks for one band of N tiles), so the bf16 read-modify-write working set of out fits in L2/MALL instead of HBM
directions.hypothesis: At 32768 the atomic RMW into a 402 MB out (bigger than the 256 MB MALL and the 4 MB per-XCD L2) costs ~390 µs, 30% of stage 2. Each token's 4 routes sit in 4 distinct expert blocks far apart in the N-fastest order, so every RMW line is fetched from HBM up to 4 times. With an outer band of 1–8 N tiles, the out slab touched is 8–64 MB (32768×BN×2 B), the W2 band per expert is small, and the gathered A (50 MB total) stays in MALL, so the atomics hit cache. Race band widths against the current order and check that error stays within bounds.
directions.priority_reason: Recovering half the measured atomic cost is ~8% at 32768, ~5% at 13152, ~4% at 10000 and ~1–2% at M. That is ~0.8% of the mean.

directions.title: Stage-2 A-stationary N sweep: each workgroup keeps its gathered A tile (≤64×768 fp4 + scales, ~25 KB) in LDS and walks several N tiles, double-buffering B across tile boundaries, to amortize the short-K per-tile fixed cost
directions.hypothesis: With K=768 a 64×128 stage-2 tile has only 3 k-steps of 256, so the A gather, B fill, LDS c-shuffle and epilogue dominate. Even without atomics stage 2 reaches only 1.38 PF/s vs stage 1's 2.9. Today the gathered A rows are re-fetched for each of the 48 N tiles (~2.4 GB of gather traffic at 32768). Loading A once per workgroup and sweeping 4–8 N tiles, with the next B tile's loads issued during the current tile's atomics, removes the repeated gathers and the pipeline drain. This differs from the ledger's persistent-grid item, which targets dispatch waste, not A reuse or cross-tile pipelining.
directions.priority_reason: Report §4.3 puts the per-tile overhead as the larger portable share of stage 2. A 10–20% stage-2 cut on 5 M/L Points is ~4–8% each, discounted for occupancy risk.

directions.title: Hide the out zero-fill at M/L: move it from the x-quant kernel into compute-bound stage 1 (each workgroup zeroes a slice after its main loop), and vectorize x-quant's 1-byte E8M0 scale stores
directions.hypothesis: At large n, x-quant plus zero-fill is 7–9% of the call at 4.0–4.6 TB/s, and the zero-fill is half its writes (402 MB at 32768, ~80 µs). It exists only for the atomic stage 2. Stage 1 runs before stage 2 on the same stream and is compute-bound at 2–2.9 PF/s, so streaming stores issued there overlap MFMA work at nearly no cost. Packing the four 1-byte scale stores per 32-element block into wider stores trims the rest. The order stays correct because stage 1 finishes before stage 2 starts, and nothing waits across workgroups.
directions.priority_reason: ~2.5–3.5% on 3 L Points and ~2% on 2 M Points, ~0 at S. That is ~0.5% of the mean.

directions.title: S-regime stage-1 memory-level parallelism: deepen W1 prefetch (more outstanding 16-byte buffer_loads per wave, an extra B stage) in the single-round 768-WG grid to push 6.3–6.6 TB/s toward ~7 TB/s
directions.category: data path / bytes in flight (S regime, stage 1)
directions.hypothesis: At n≤640, stage 1 is exactly one round (768 WGs at 3 WG/CU, 142 VGPRs), so the grid cannot add parallelism. The only way to keep more HBM requests in flight is more outstanding loads per wave. Stage 1 is ~100 µs of a ~175 µs call against a 146 µs practical floor. A 5% rate gain is ~5 µs per Point. Check against waitcnt stalls in the ISA and the VGPR count, so the change does not drop occupancy.
directions.priority_reason: Up to ~2–3% per S Point if the rate rises 5%. Discounted because 6.6 TB/s already beats every stream kernel measured here (≤5.8 TB/s).
